analysis.one_liner: Lets victims of securities fraud sue for triple damages under federal racketeering law.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in January 2002, sent to its Crime subcommittee in March, and died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5][S1].
analysis.plain_summary: Federal racketeering law lets fraud victims sue for triple their damages and their attorney's fees, but a special carve-out blocks investors from using it for securities fraud [S3]. This bill would strike that carve-out, so people who lose money to stock fraud could bring racketeering suits against the companies and executives that defrauded them [S2][S3]. It was introduced in late January 2002, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to its Crime subcommittee in March, and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors and pension holders who lose money to securities fraud. They could recover triple their actual damages and get their attorney's fees paid, instead of recovering only actual losses (or nothing) through the slower, weaker private securities lawsuit process.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors and pension holders defrauded by stock scams

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the securities-fraud carve-out from the civil racketeering remedy in 18 U.S.C. 1964(c), which currently bars anyone from relying on securities fraud as the basis for a civil racketeering claim [S3].
Repealing the denial of civil remedies would allow private plaintiffs injured by securities fraud to bring civil racketeering suits, which carry treble damages and attorney's fees [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Securities firms, investment banks, and officers of publicly traded companies, who would face exposure to triple-damages racketeering suits when they commit stock fraud. Some of that litigation cost would pass through to all shareholders in the form of higher insurance and defense costs.

drawbacks.text: Opening the broad civil racketeering remedy to ordinary securities disputes could encourage sprawling, drawn-out lawsuits against companies whose conduct falls short of serious fraud, raising defense and insurance costs that shareholders ultimately bear.
The change rides on the existing fraud requirements of the securities laws, so its real-world deterrent value would depend on how aggressively courts and the SEC police fraud in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: treble damages and fee-shifting give defrauded investors a strong private deterrent against corporate fraud, at a moment when billion-dollar accounting scandals were dominating the news. The cost is that a blunt racketeering remedy aimed at ordinary securities disputes can generate expensive, abusive litigation, so a careful design would need limits. On balance, the bill addressed a genuine gap in investor protection, and the way to handle the litigation concern is through drafting limits, not by leaving the carve-out in place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee and then in its Crime subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers (D-MI) introduced the Securities Fraud Prevention Act of 2002 on January 29, 2002, joined as original cosponsors by House Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt and six other members [S3][S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced [S5].
On March 18, 2002, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 with the bill still parked in subcommittee; it was never scheduled for a hearing or a vote [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Securities firms, investment banks, and corporate officers benefited, because the carve-out that shields them from triple-damages racketeering suits stayed in force. Investors who lose money to stock fraud remained without that remedy.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers, Jr.
for.role: Ranking Member, House Judiciary Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to his own committee's jurisdiction, where it stalled.

for.name: Rep. Richard Gephardt
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill on the day it was introduced.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner, Jr. (R-WI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after receiving the bill; never scheduled a hearing or markup in the eleven months it had jurisdiction.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Crime
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 18, 2002 and held no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's sole Independent; no Republican signed on, and with no vote ever held the partisan split on the floor is unknown.

industries.industry: Securities firms, investment banks, and publicly traded companies' officers and directors
industries.note: The bill would have stripped their statutory shield from treble-damages racketeering suits, so executives and firms that commit stock fraud could no longer be sued for triple the harm they cause. The carve-out's continuation is the reason investors who are defrauded recover less. Sources: the bill text and summary [S3][S2].

industries.industry: Securities litigation and class-action plaintiffs' bar
industries.note: Attorney's-fee provisions under the civil racketeering remedy would create a new pool of securities-fraud cases for plaintiffs' lawyers, whose fees would be paid by defendants when they win.
